section: Clear information. Honest limits. No promotion.
originalContent:
Every person considering breast enhancement has different anatomy, breast tissue, aesthetic preferences and expectations. This website exists to explain the options before you discuss them with any clinic or surgeon.

We aim to make complex treatment choices easier to understand by presenting the potential benefits, limitations, recovery considerations and risks of each approach — so you can make decisions grounded in accurate information rather than promotion.

Whether you are exploring breast augmentation surgery, fat transfer or a non-surgical treatment, our focus is on transparent, evidence-based information and realistic expectations.

originalContent.title: Breast Implants: Types, Placement & Long-Term Reality
originalContent.introduction: Breast implants are medical devices placed surgically to increase breast volume. They are the most studied enlargement method — with real complication and revision rates that every patient should understand before deciding.

page: Breast Implants: Types, Placement & Long-Term Reality
section: prose / educational figure

originalContent.html: An implant is a device — a shell filled with saline (sterile salt water) or silicone gel — placed behind the breast tissue or behind the pectoral muscle. Implant surgery is the best-documented route to a larger, predictable breast size, but it is surgery: it carries risks, it is not permanent, and follow-up over the years is part of the decision.

originalContent.title: Non-Surgical Breast Enhancement: Options & Safety
originalContent.introduction: Non-surgical treatments differ widely in their intended effects, evidence and regulatory status. This section explains those differences clearly, without advertising claims.

section: Six questions worth asking

originalContent.title: What is the exact product and intended use?
originalContent.text: Ask for the precise product name, its approved indications and whether breast use is authorised in your jurisdiction.

originalContent.title: Is it approved for this purpose?
originalContent.text: Facial approval does not imply approval for injection into the breasts. Products and permitted uses vary by country.

originalContent.title: What does the evidence actually show?
originalContent.text: Distinguish marketing claims from peer-reviewed evidence for the specific procedure being offered.

originalContent.title: Who is performing it, and with what competence?
originalContent.text: Suitability depends on the precise product, intended use, clinician competence and applicable regulation.

originalContent.title: What are the risks and possible complications?
originalContent.text: Ask about infection, pain, tissue damage, nodules, asymmetry and how complications would be managed.

originalContent.title: What are the alternatives?
originalContent.text: Consider evidence-based alternatives for increasing breast volume, including surgical options where relevant.

section: Page banner

originalContent.title: Breast Fillers: Safety, Evidence & Alternatives
originalContent.introduction: Dermal fillers are injectable products used for certain approved aesthetic indications. Their use for breast enlargement is a different matter and is not established, approved or routine.

section: Page banner

originalContent.title: Breast Thread Procedures: Uses & Limitations
originalContent.introduction: Thread procedures use medical sutures placed in tissue for specific intended effects. Different thread materials, designs and placement techniques have different indications and limitations.

section: prose / educational figure

originalContent.html:
Understanding thread-based procedures

Thread-based procedures are not, on current evidence, a predictable alternative to breast surgery. Threads should not be presented as established substitutes for breast augmentation.

Potential risks include infection, discomfort, visible or palpable threads, asymmetry, thread migration or extrusion, and the need for corrective treatment. Suitability depends on the precise product, intended use, clinician competence and applicable regulations.

section: Page banner

originalContent.title: Mono Threads: Uses and Limitations
originalContent.introduction: Mono threads differ from cog threads in design and intended mechanical effect. These differences matter when assessing suitability and realistic outcomes.

section: prose / educational figure

originalContent.html: Mono threads are fine threads used in aesthetics for particular intended effects. They should not be claimed to reliably enlarge the breast without suitable evidence. As with all thread procedures, the intended effect is defined by the specific product and technique.

page: PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained
section: Page banner

originalContent.title: PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained
originalContent.introduction: Platelet-rich plasma is prepared from your own blood to concentrate platelets. Its effects depend entirely on the specific indication and the evidence available for it.

page: PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained
section: prose / educational figure

originalContent.html:
How PRP is prepared

PRP is prepared by taking a sample of the patient’s own blood and processing it to concentrate the platelets. The resulting preparation is intended for specific purposes; those purposes are not interchangeable, and a preparation intended for one indication is not automatically appropriate for another.

PRP and breast enhancement

Claims about PRP and breast enhancement should be assessed against appropriate clinical evidence for the precise procedure being offered. The evidence for a particular use should be established before that use is described as effective.

section: Page banner

originalContent.title: Biostimulators: Collagen-Stimulating Treatments
originalContent.introduction: Biostimulators are a broad category of products intended to stimulate a tissue response, such as collagen production, for selected indications. Their ingredients, mechanisms, authorised uses and safety profiles vary considerably.

page: Sculptra and PLLA: Uses, Safety & Evidence
section: Page banner

originalContent.title: Sculptra and PLLA: Uses, Safety & Evidence
originalContent.introduction: Sculptra is a poly-L-lactic acid-based injectable used for certain specified aesthetic indications, subject to product labelling and local authorisation. It should not be described as a proven breast-enlargement product.

section: Page banner

originalContent.title: Stem Cells and Regenerative Medicine

section: How to check a surgeon before you commit

originalContent.title: Confirm registration
originalContent.text: Find the surgeon on your national medical council or regulator and confirm the registration is current and unrestricted.

originalContent.title: Confirm surgical training
originalContent.text: A surgeon performing breast surgery should hold recognised training in plastic or reconstructive surgery, not merely a short cosmetic course.

originalContent.title: Check scope of practice
originalContent.text: The clinician should operate within their qualifications; ask directly who will perform each part of the procedure.

originalContent.title: Check the operating setting
originalContent.text: Ask where the procedure is performed, who provides anaesthesia, and what arrangements exist for emergencies.

originalContent.title: Ask for the plan in writing
originalContent.text: A reputable surgeon provides a written plan covering technique, risks, costs and revision policy — so you can think it over.
